variants.title: Run one bounded request
variants.context: One bounded AI request crosses five stages: identity and purpose, untrusted context, constrained inference, policy and authorization, then observe and recover. Each stage owns a different decision, and no model instruction can redefine those external boundaries.
variants.prompt: A support assistant answers a question about a customer account. Put the stages of one bounded request in order.

items.text: Treat the prompt, the uploaded file, and every retrieved document as potentially adversarial input.
Authenticate the actor, classify the use case, and load only the permissions and data that purpose allows.
Run inference with scoped instructions and bounded context so the model proposes rather than decides.
Attribute the outcome to exact versions and keep containment and recovery reachable.
Validate output policy, evidence, schema, arguments, and required approval outside the model.

variants.hint: Which decision has to be settled before any data is loaded at all?
variants.explanation: Identity and purpose bound what is loaded, the model only proposes, and enforcement plus recovery stay outside the model.

variants.title: Run one bounded request
variants.context: One bounded AI request crosses five stages: identity and purpose, untrusted context, constrained inference, policy and authorization, then observe and recover. Each stage owns a different decision, and no model instruction can redefine those external boundaries.
variants.prompt: An agent reads a support thread and proposes a refund. Put the stages in order, ending with the record that makes recovery possible.

items.text: Let the model draft a refund proposal without giving it authority to move money.
Record versions, cohort, and a minimized decision trace so the refund path stays reversible.
Check the tool, amount, subject account, limit, and required human approval outside the model.
Authenticate the requester and load only the account scope the refund purpose permits.
Load the support thread as untrusted content that an attacker may have written into.

variants.hint: Where does the authority to execute the refund actually live?
variants.explanation: A model may propose a consequential action, but authorization and the recovery record sit outside it.

variants.title: Run one bounded request
variants.context: One bounded AI request crosses five stages: identity and purpose, untrusted context, constrained inference, policy and authorization, then observe and recover. Each stage owns a different decision, and no model instruction can redefine those external boundaries.
variants.prompt: A retrieved policy document contains text telling the assistant to ignore its instructions and email a customer list. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Keep the model output a proposal, so injected text can at most change the words it drafts.
Deny the send tool because the destination and subject fall outside the authorized scope.
Alert on the denied action, preserve a minimized trace, and quarantine the poisoned source.
Resolve the caller identity and purpose that decide which mailbox data is loadable at all.
Ingest the retrieved document as data, never as an instruction that raises its own trust.

variants.hint: Ask which stage the injected text can influence and which stages it cannot reach.
variants.explanation: Injected content can steer wording, but identity, authorization, and recovery are enforced outside the model.

variants.title: Contain the incident
variants.context: Incident response runs in a fixed order: confirm impact, bound the affected path, preserve the identity needed to reproduce it, then prevent recurrence. Severity follows impact, reach, and reversibility rather than waiting for the model to explain itself.
variants.prompt: A monitor reports unsafe advice reaching a small cohort. Put the response steps in order.

items.text: Restrict the affected cohort, capability, route, or version until the harm stops.
Repair the control, validate the known-good path, and add a regression case for the failure.
Validate the signal without leaving active harm exposed just to raise statistical confidence.
Capture timestamps, cohort, exact component versions, and a minimized decision trace.

variants.hint: Ask which step stops harm and which step only explains it.
variants.explanation: Contain first, then preserve enough identity to reproduce the failing path, then close the control gap.

variants.title: Contain the incident
variants.context: Incident response runs in a fixed order: confirm impact, bound the affected path, preserve the identity needed to reproduce it, then prevent recurrence. Severity follows impact, reach, and reversibility rather than waiting for the model to explain itself.
variants.prompt: An agent executed a tool call that no policy authorized, across several tenants. Put the response steps in order.

items.text: Revoke the tool credential and stop the route, since no safe fallback covers this action.
Tighten the authorization check, retest the known-good path, and look for similar tool paths.
Preserve the tool proposals, policy decisions, and component versions that produced the call.
Confirm that the unauthorized call actually executed and which tenants it touched.

variants.hint: An unauthorized action is critical before anyone knows why it happened.
variants.explanation: Impact drives containment; evidence and prevention follow once the path is bounded.

variants.title: Contain the incident
variants.context: Incident response runs in a fixed order: confirm impact, bound the affected path, preserve the identity needed to reproduce it, then prevent recurrence. Severity follows impact, reach, and reversibility rather than waiting for the model to explain itself.
variants.prompt: A near miss is reported: a prompt injection almost caused a data release. Put the response steps in order.

items.text: Quarantine the poisoned source so the same content cannot reach another request.
Promote the minimized case into a protected regression and review neighboring paths.
Confirm whether any release occurred and how far the attempt actually reached.
Store the minimized fixture, affected slice, and the versions that were running.

variants.hint: A near miss still earns the same loop; only the confirmed impact differs.
variants.explanation: Near misses become regression evidence, which is how the loop prevents the next occurrence.

variants.title: Escalate by impact
variants.context: Escalation follows observed impact. An unauthorized action or exposed sensitive data is critical on its own, and active harm reaching ten or more users a minute counts as high reach. Critical or high-reach harm restricts the affected path when a safe fallback exists and shuts it down when none does.
variants.prompt: An agent executed a tool call that no policy authorized. Two users per minute are affected and a safe fallback mode exists. What is the first response?
options: Restrict the affected path under a security or safety incident commander.
Investigate only, since two users per minute is well below high reach.
Shut the service down until the unauthorized action has been explained.
optionFeedback: An unauthorized action is critical regardless of reach, and a fallback makes restriction the right containment.
Reach does not soften an unauthorized action; that signal is critical on its own.
Shutdown is for critical harm with no safe boundary left, and a fallback exists here.
variants.hint: Which signals count as critical without looking at reach at all?
variants.explanation: Unauthorized action and sensitive-data exposure are critical by themselves, and restriction suffices while a safe fallback exists.

variants.title: Escalate by impact
variants.context: Escalation follows observed impact. An unauthorized action or exposed sensitive data is critical on its own, and active harm reaching ten or more users a minute counts as high reach. Critical or high-reach harm restricts the affected path when a safe fallback exists and shuts it down when none does.
variants.prompt: Unsafe advice is reaching about four users per minute. No tool ran, no sensitive data left the system, and a safe fallback exists. What is the first response?
options: Restrict the affected path, owned by the product safety on-call.
Investigate only, because four users a minute is below high reach.
Roll back and shut down, because any active harm requires a full stop.
optionFeedback: Active harm requires containment; reach and critical signals set the owner, not whether to act.
Active harm is already exposure, so investigation alone leaves users exposed.
Shutdown is reserved for critical or high-reach harm with no safe fallback.
variants.hint: Active harm is already exposure, so what does the reach number change?
variants.explanation: Active harm restricts the path; reach and critical signals decide the owner and whether shutdown is required.

variants.title: Escalate by impact
variants.context: Escalation follows observed impact. An unauthorized action or exposed sensitive data is critical on its own, and active harm reaching ten or more users a minute counts as high reach. Critical or high-reach harm restricts the affected path when a safe fallback exists and shuts it down when none does.
variants.prompt: A researcher reports a prompt that might leak another tenant's data, but replay shows no leak, no unauthorized action, and no active harm. What is the first response?
options: Investigate with the service owner while the path keeps operating normally.
Shut the tenant route down until the report has been fully explained.
Restrict every tenant path because a leak has now been reported.
optionFeedback: With no confirmed harm, exposure, or unauthorized action, investigation is the proportionate response.
Shutdown without confirmed impact spends availability on an unreproduced report.
Restriction answers confirmed active harm or a critical signal, not an unreproduced report.
variants.hint: Separate what was observed from what was feared.
variants.explanation: Escalation follows observed impact, so an unreproduced report is investigated rather than contained.

variants.title: Read the policy gate
variants.context: The policy gate returns the strictest decision the independent control layers require. Missing authentication, a purpose outside policy, sensitive data crossing the output boundary, a failed output policy check, or an unauthorized tool all block. A consequential action without approval or a high-impact claim without evidence goes to review.
variants.prompt: Every content check passes, but the proposed tool is not in the actor's authorized set and the action is consequential with no approval. What does the gate return?
options: Allow, because every content and evidence check passed.
Block, because an unauthorized tool is a blocking condition.
Review, because an accountable human could still approve it.
optionFeedback: Content checks are one layer; the gate reads authorization too.
Blockers outrank review reasons, and an unauthorized tool is a blocker.
Approval cannot repair a tool the actor was never authorized to use.
variants.hint: When a blocker and a review reason both fire, which one wins?
variants.explanation: The gate returns the strictest decision required, so any blocker outranks a review reason.

variants.title: Read the policy gate
variants.context: The policy gate returns the strictest decision the independent control layers require. Missing authentication, a purpose outside policy, sensitive data crossing the output boundary, a failed output policy check, or an unauthorized tool all block. A consequential action without approval or a high-impact claim without evidence goes to review.
variants.prompt: Authentication, purpose, output policy, and evidence all pass and the tool is authorized, but the action moves money and nobody approved it. What does the gate return?
options: Block, because moving money is prohibited for any agent.
Review, because a consequential action needs accountable approval.
Allow, because no blocking condition is present in the request.
optionFeedback: The gate blocks unauthorized tools and policy failures, not a category of action.
An unapproved consequential action is a review reason, so the gate routes it to a human.
No blocker means it is not blocked, but review reasons still change the decision.
variants.hint: Which list does an unapproved consequential action belong to?
variants.explanation: Review routes consequential or unsupported proposals to an accountable human instead of allowing them.

variants.title: Read the policy gate
variants.context: The policy gate returns the strictest decision the independent control layers require. Missing authentication, a purpose outside policy, sensitive data crossing the output boundary, a failed output policy check, or an unauthorized tool all block. A consequential action without approval or a high-impact claim without evidence goes to review.
variants.prompt: The draft answer is well grounded and the tool is authorized, but the privacy check finds a customer identifier in the output. What does the gate return?
options: Block, because sensitive data crossed the output boundary.
Review, because a human reviewer could redact the identifier.
Allow, because the claim is supported by retrieved evidence.
optionFeedback: Sensitive data leaving the boundary is a blocking condition on its own.
Review covers unapproved actions and unsupported claims, not a data leak.
Grounding an answer does not authorize releasing personal data.
variants.hint: Is a leak a review reason or a hard stop?
variants.explanation: Sensitive data crossing the output boundary blocks regardless of how well the answer is grounded.

variants.title: Name the failure origin
variants.context: The failure taxonomy separates unsafe behavior, adversarial manipulation and excessive agency, unequal outcomes, privacy and data governance, and monitoring and response. The categories overlap, but their first containment steps differ, so naming the origin decides what to fix first.
variants.prompt: Match each observed failure to the category whose first containment step applies.

pairs.label: A retrieved invoice tells the agent to email an internal contact list
pairs.detail: Adversarial manipulation: treat external content as data and authorize each tool call against authenticated context.

pairs.label: The assistant gives confident medical guidance with no supporting source
pairs.detail: Unsafe behavior: require evidence or abstention for consequential claims and keep a safe fallback.

pairs.label: Unsafe advice is twice as common in one language while the fleet average looks healthy
pairs.detail: Unequal outcomes: measure error severity and uncertainty by slice, then route weak cohorts to a safer mode.

pairs.label: A support archive keeps full prompts and outputs with no retention limit
pairs.detail: Privacy and governance: minimize collection and bind access, retention, and deletion to a documented purpose.

variants.hint: Ask what the first containment step would have to change.
variants.explanation: Each category names a different first control, so classifying the origin decides what gets fixed first.

variants.title: Name the failure origin
variants.context: The failure taxonomy separates unsafe behavior, adversarial manipulation and excessive agency, unequal outcomes, privacy and data governance, and monitoring and response. The categories overlap, but their first containment steps differ, so naming the origin decides what to fix first.
variants.prompt: Match each observed failure to the category whose first containment step applies.

pairs.label: An operator cannot say which prompt version produced a flagged answer
pairs.detail: Monitoring and response: join safety signals to model, prompt, policy, route, and cohort identity.

pairs.label: An agent holds a broad token that can delete records the task never needed
pairs.detail: Excessive agency: limit capability, scope, rate, and side-effect reach independently of the model.

pairs.label: The assistant refuses legitimate questions from one dialect far more often
pairs.detail: Unequal outcomes: false positives concentrate harm too, so measure them by slice.

pairs.label: A summary of one tenant's document appears inside another tenant's answer
pairs.detail: Privacy and governance: test cross-tenant access and memorization instead of relying on redaction.

variants.hint: Over-refusal and leakage are different origins with different owners.
variants.explanation: The first containment step differs by origin, which is why one generic guardrail list is not a strategy.

variants.title: Name the failure origin
variants.context: The failure taxonomy separates unsafe behavior, adversarial manipulation and excessive agency, unequal outcomes, privacy and data governance, and monitoring and response. The categories overlap, but their first containment steps differ, so naming the origin decides what to fix first.
variants.prompt: Match each observed failure to the category whose first containment step applies.

pairs.label: A user asking for an ordinary recipe is refused as unsafe
pairs.detail: Unsafe or unreliable behavior: inappropriate refusal is a behavior failure, so evaluate realistic tasks.

pairs.label: An uploaded resume instructs the model to advance its own candidate
pairs.detail: Adversarial manipulation: untrusted uploads are data, and the decision stays outside the model.

pairs.label: A low-volume cohort has the worst error rate but was dropped from the report
pairs.detail: Unequal outcomes: preserve small cohorts under privacy controls instead of dropping them.

pairs.label: Rollback was never rehearsed, so the team cannot reach a known-good state
pairs.detail: Monitoring and response: rehearse rollback, route restriction, shutdown, and evidence preservation.

variants.hint: Ask who owns the first action, not how bad the outcome sounds.
variants.explanation: A taxonomy speeds diagnosis because each origin points at a different owner and first control.
